Assessment and Care of

& Testing

APGAR SCORING
 Quick assessment done to evaluate the newborn’s transition 
from intrauterine life to extrauterine life.
 Establish hemodynamic stability

APGAR SCORING
 1 minute & 5 minutes
 Initial Assessment of Newborn Status after birth
 Assesses the process of transition to extra uterine life
 Respiratory changes are most critical
 Neonatal renal, neurologic, endocrine & cardiac 
systems are fully functioning in utero
 Respiratory and GI systems must become functional

APGAR SCORING
0 1 2
Heart Rate Absent Slow (<100bpm) Normal (>100bpm)
Respiratory Effort Absent Slow, irregular 
weak cry
 Good cry
Muscle tone Flaccid Some flexion Active
Reflexes No Response Weak cry/ grimace Vigorous cry
Color Blue, pale Body pink, 
extremities blue
Completely pink

Transition to Extrauterine Life 
 First period of reactivity
 Lasts up to 30 minutes after birth
 Newborn’s heart rate increases to 160 to 180 beats/min
 Decreases after 30 minutes
 Decrease in motor activity after period

Transition to Extrauterine Life—cont’d 
 Second period of reactivity
 Occurs 4 to 8 hours after birth
 Tachycardia, tachypnea occur
 Meconium passed 
 Increased muscle tone, changes in skin 
color becomes pinker, and mucous 
production

Physiologic Adaptations 
 Respiratory system
 Initiation of breathing
 Vaginal birth:  fluid in lungs “squeezed out”
 Change in pressure and other stimuli causes air 
to “rush in” to the lungs
 Chemoreceptors and carotid bodies stimulate 
respirations
 Normal breathing:  irregular, 30-60 per minute
 Neonate periods of apnea of less than 20 
seconds are normal

Physiologic Adaptations—cont’d 
 Respiratory system
 Signs of respiratory distress
 Grunting-audible grunting
 Retracting-sub-sternal retractions-visualization of xiphoid process 
or  rib cage
 Cyanosis 
 Maintaining adequate oxygen supply
 Combination effect of respirations, oxygen demand glucose 
control and temperature

Physiologic Adaptations—cont’d 
 Cardiovascular system
 Change from fetal to “newborn” circulation
 Closure of patent ducts due to pressure changes and 
function of lungs
 Decreased pulmonary resistance
 Increased pressure in L ventricle
 Murmurs may persist
 Heart rate and sounds
 120-160
 Auscultate apical one full minute

Figure 4-11    Fetal circulation. Blood leaves the placenta and enters the fetus through the 
umbilical vein. After circulating through the fetus, the blood returns to the placenta through 
the umbilical arteries. The ductus venosus, the foramen ovale, and the ductus arteriosus 
allow the blood to bypass the fetal liver and lungs.

Physiologic Adaptations—cont’d 
 Cardiovascular
 Blood pressure
 60-80 / 40-50
 Not routinely done
 Thermogenic System
 Maintaining heat is critical for newborn
 Thermogenesis
 No shivering mechanism
 Maintain heat by metabolism of brown fat
 Triggered by activity in brain, heart & liver
 Heat loss
 Temperature regulation
 Normal temperature:  36.5 – 37.2 (97.7-99.7)
 Axillary temp

Effects of cold stress. When an infant is stressed by cold, oxygen consumption increases and 
pulmonary and peripheral vasoconstriction occur, thereby decreasing oxygen uptake by the 
lungs and oxygen to the tissues; anaerobic glycolysis increases; and there is a decrease in Po2 
and pH, leading to metabolic acidosis.

Physiologic Adaptations
 Renal system
 Inability to concentrate urine (3mos)
 Immature ability to regulate bicarb 
 Fluid and electrolyte: excess amount in 
extracellular fluid

Physiologic Adaptations—cont’d 
 Gastrointestinal system
 No bacteria in GI tract: cannot make vitamin K yet
 Stomach capacity 30-90 mL
 Stools
 Meconium:  amniotic fluid, bilirubin, mucosal cells
 Pass within 12-24 hrs:  up to 48 hrs
 Transitional Stool:  day 3:  greenish brown – yellowish 
brown; thin & sticky
 Milk Stool:  day 4:  breastfed:  yellow – gold; pasty; formula: 
yellow to light brown, firmer, smelly

Physiologic Adaptations—cont’d 
 Hepatic system
 Iron storage full developed by 4-6 months 
 Carbohydrate metabolism
 MAKES OWN INSULIN
 Infants of GDM or DM mothers at risk for hypoglycemia
 Depletion of glycogen stores within 24 hrs
 Jaundice
 Bilirubin (breakdown of RBC) in skin
 Physiologic phenomenon:  after 24 hrs of life
 Earlier jaundice can be pathologic and require treatment
 Related to ABO/Rh incompatibility with mother 
 Immune system: no IgA – mucosal immunity 
exposure to pathogens not developed

Assessment for Congenital Anomalies (18.4)
Finding
 Polyhydramnios 
 Oligohydramnios
 Distended Abdomen
 Empty Abdomen
 Unable to insert NGT-nares
 Unable to insert NGT-stomach
 > 20 mL of fluid NGT aspiration
 Failure to pass meconium
 Delayed passing of mec >24 
hours
 ONE umbilical artery
Possible Anomaly 
 Gastrointestinal 
 GU or prematurity
 Ascities or Tumor
 Diaphragmatic hernia
 Choanal atresis
 Esophageal atresia
 Duodenal or ileal atresia
 Imperforate anus
 Hirschprung disease
 R/O congenital renal or cardiac 
or chromosomal trisomy

Assessment
 General Survey
 Color-pink, acrocyanosis: resolves in 24 hours
 Position and muscle tone- flexed
 Weight: 2500 – 4000 gm (5lbs 8oz – 8lbs 13oz)
 <2500 SGA >4000 LGA
 Lose 5-10% in first 3-5 days
 Length  45-55 cm
 Vital Signs
 TPR
 36.5-37.2; 110-160; 30-60
 BP 60/80 
 Pulse Ox > 95%

Assessment – cont’d
 Face
 Symmetry-asymmetry may indicate genetic problems
 Eyes:  in line w ears
 Ears: tags/ sinus/ position/ cartilage
 Nose: patent
 Mouth: symmetry w cry
 Palate: intact-smooth rounded arch not pitched or open
 Gums: presence / absence teeth/ Epsteins pearls

Assessment – cont’d
 General
 Chest: shape measure cms 
 Abdomen: shape measure cms
 Umbilical cord:  3 vessels; clamp
 AVA=2 arteries and 1 vein
 Extremities 
 Motion, position (flexion)

Assessment 
Head & Skin
 Fontanelles – open & flat (bulging = increased ICP)
 Caput succedaneum
 Cephalhematoma
 Desquamation-dry peeling skin
 Mongolian spots-most common in Asian, Hispanic or African 
American infants-point them out to parents
 Lanugo-fine hair covering fetus, generally goes 
 Millia-white spots on nose- don’t treat not acne
 Nevus vasculosus- overgrowth of capillaries 
 Erythema toxicum- rash of neonate, benign self limiting
 Harlequin sign-half of face turns red-may occur with lying on one side
 Vernix caseosa
 Stork bites or salmon patches
Fig. 24-5. A, Telangiectatic nevi (stork bite). B, Erythema toxicum.

Physiologic Adaptations—cont’d
 Head
 Circumference
 Larger than chest 1- 2 cms larger
 Smaller than chest indication for evaluation of microcephaly
 Differences may be due to molding
 Shape
 Anterior fontanelle
 Diamond shaped
 Closes at 18 mos
 Posterior fontanelle
 Triangle shaped
 Closes 8-12 wks

when molding is present.

Physiologic Adaptations—cont’d 
 Caput Succedaneum
 Generalized edema of scalp
 “molding”
 Resolves 3-4 days
 Cephalohematoma
 Collection of blood between skull bone and periosteum
 Does NOT cross suture line
Fig. 24-3. A, Caput succedaneum. B, Subgaleal hemorrhage. C, Cephalhematoma.

Assessing Skin
 General Skin:
 Creases in hands/ feet
 Simian crease:  single palmar crease = Downs
 Plantar creases = gestational age
 Desquamation/peeling normal to some degree  
 late term very deep cracks

Physiologic Adaptations—cont’d 
 Mongolian Spots
 Bluish black pigment
 Buttocks/back
 Nevi
 Stork bites telangiectatic nevi
 Blanch when press & fade
 Hemangioma 
 Erythema Toxicum: normal rash

Reproductive system
Female
 Examine genitalia
 Skin tag a
 Discharge: pseudo-menses
 Both Male & Female

 From maternal estrogen
 Discharge

nipples

 hypospadias  vs  epispadias
 Foreskin
 not retractable
 Testes: may still be

Assessment-cont’d
 Skeletal system
 At birth more cartilage then ossified bone
 Extremities:  position, ROM
 Assessment of hips & feet
 Ortolani maneuver-hip dysplasia 
 Galeazzi Sign- asymmetrical gluteal folds
 Club foot
 polydactyly

Fig. 24-8. Signs of developmental dysplasia of the hip. A, Asymmetry of gluteal and thigh folds 
with shortening of the thigh (Galeazzi sign). B, Limited hip abduction, as seen in flexion (Ortolani 
test). C, Apparent shortening of the femur, as indicated by the level of the knees in flexion (Allis 
sign). D, Ortolani test with femoral head moving in and out of acetabulum (in infants 1 to 2 
months old).

Assessment- cont’d
 Neuromuscular system
 Newborn reflexes
 Neurologic assessment

Reflex Assessment
 Rooting
 Turns head toward stimulus and opens mouth
 Sucking & Swallowing
 Grasp
 Hands and feet
 Moro
 “startle” :  extension of arms and legs w/ stimuli
 Babinski
 Hyperextension w flexion of toe (up to 1 yr)
 Stepping
 Tonic Neck (fencing)

Behavioral Characteristics 
 Sleep-wake states

newborns

 Medication

Routine Newborn Care
 Daily Assessment and Documentation
 Vital signs- Pulse, Resp., Temp
 Weight 
 Diaper care
 Voiding / stooling
 Feeding pattern
 Family attachment

Routine Newborn Care
 Weight and VS assessment daily
 Temperature stabilization
 “wrap” in open isolette
 May lose 5-10% of birth weight
 Important to assess feeding pattern 
 Important to assess void / stool pattern
 Skin assessment
 Color assessment:  jaundice

Umbilical Cord Care
 Hospital protocol determines technique for cord care
 Cochrane review of 21 studies: no difference in dry cord 
compared with those treated with antiseptics
 Natural healing, soap and water, alcohol, or povidone-
iodine
 Clamp is removed once the stump is dry
 Falls off appx 10 days

Procedures & Laboratory Testing
 Eye Prophylaxis
 Administration of erythromycin and tetracycline 
antibiotic ointment for prevention of opthalmia 
neonatorum-STI from mother during birth
 Administer within 1-2 hours of birth
 Vitamin K
 0.5 – 1 mg IM X 1 dose shortly after birth anterior thigh-
vastus lateralis
 Produced in GI tract from bacteria– need PO food to 
produce

Procedures & Laboratory Testing
 Hepatitis B Vaccine
 Prior to discharge from newborn nursery
 At one month of age
 Hepatitis B Immune Globulin 
 HBIG administered within 12 hours of birth if mom is Heb 
B positive- BEFORE discharge
 2nd dose at 3 mos
 3rd dose at 6 mos

Procedures & Laboratory Testing
 Glucose- SGA, GDM and LGA infants (>4000 gm)
 Hourly heel stick

 Blood type- only if indicated (maternal type)
 Indirect coombs test-presence of antibodies in maternal serum
 Direct coombs test-presence of hemolytic disease in newborn
 Bilirubin- transcutaneous and serum if symptomatic
 Metabolic Screening: State mandate

Circumcision

Fig. 25-14. Technique of circumcision. A to D, Prepuce is stripped and slit to facilitate its 
retraction behind glans penis. E, Prepuce is now clamped and excessive prepuce cut off. 
F and G, A very small needle with plain 2- or 3- catgut is used for suturing; some 
physicians prefer silk.

Post Circumcision Care
 Observe for first void
 Observe for bleeding
 Careful diaper change
 Application of vaseline/neosporin
 Heals within 10 days

Initial Newborn Assessments 
 Signs indicating a problem
 Nasal flaring, chest retractions
 Grunting on exhalation, labored breathing
 Generalized cyanosis, flaccid body posture
 Abnormal breath sounds, abnormal respiratory rates
 Abnormal heart rates, abnormal newborn size

Initial Newborn Assessments (cont’d.)
 Apgar scoring (see Table 18.1)
 Length and weight, vital signs (see Table 18.2)
 Gestational age assessment (see Figure 18.3)
 Physical maturity (skin texture, lanugo, plantar creases, breast 
tissue, eyes & ears, genitals)
 Neuromuscular maturity (posture, square window, arm recoil, 
popliteal angle, scarf sign, heel-to-ear)

Gestational Age
 Preterm or premature: prior to 37 weeks’ gestation
 Term: 38 to 42 weeks’ gestation
 Postterm or postdates: after week 42 gestation
 Postmature: after week 42 gestation/placental aging
 Older placenta decreases in function = decreased oxygen and nutrient 
transport.
 Small for gestational age (SGA) 2500 gms (5lbs 8 oz) or below 10th 
percentile for gestational age
 Appropriate for gestational age (AGA) 
 Large for gestational age (LGA)

Ballard Gestational Age Assessment

Ballard Scoring Criteria 
 Posture—How does the newborn hold his or her extremities in relation to the trunk? The greater the degree of flexion, the greater the maturity. For example, extension of arms and legs is scored as 0 points and full flexion of 
arms and legs is scored as 4 points.
 Square window—How far can the newborn’s hands be flexed toward the wrist? The angle is measured and scored from more than 90 degrees to 0 degrees to determine the maturity rating. As the angle decreases, the 
newborn’s maturity increases. For example, an angle of more than 90 degrees is scored as –1 point and an angle 
of 0 degrees is scored as 4 points.
 Arm recoil—How far do the newborn’s arms “spring back” to a flexed position? This measure evaluates the degree of arm flexion and the strength of recoil. The reaction of the arm is then scored from 0 to 4 points based 
on the degree of flexion as the arms are returned to their normal flexed position. The higher the points 
assigned, the greater the neuromuscular maturity (for example, recoil less than a 90-degree angle is scored as 4 
points).
 Popliteal angle—How far will the newborn’s knees extend? The angle created when the knee is extended is measured. An angle of less than 90 degrees indicates greater maturity. For example, an angle of 180 degrees is 
scored as –1 point and an angle of less than 90 degrees is scored as 5 points.
 Scarf sign—How far can the elbows be moved across the newborn’s chest? An elbow that does not reach midline indicates greater maturity. For example, if the elbow reaches or nears the level of the opposite shoulder, 
this is scored as –1 point; if the elbow does not cross the proximate axillary line, it is scored as 4 points.
 Heel to ear—How close can the newborn’s feet be moved to the ears? This maneuver assesses hip flexibility: the lesser the flexibility, the greater the newborn’s maturity. The heel-to-ear assessment is scored in the same 
manner as the scarf sign.

Nursing Interventions: Immediate Newborn Period
 Maintaining airway patency
 Ensuring proper identification
 Administering prescribed medications (see Drug Guide 18.1)
 Vitamin K
 Eye prophylaxis
 Maintaining thermoregulation

Variations in Head Size and Shape in the Newborn
 Variations
 Molding
 Caput succedaneum
 Cephalhematoma
 Abnormalities
 Microcephaly
 Macrocephaly
 Large, small, or closed fontanels

Nursing Interventions for Transient Tachypnea of Newborn
 Providing oxygen-via “blow-by”  
 Ensuring warmth
 Observing respiratory status frequently
 Allowing time for pulmonary capillaries (increased fluid 
re-absorption with alveoli pressure) and the lymphatics 
to remove the remaining fluid

Selected Screening for Newborns
 PKU-Phenylketonuria: Required by law
 Education- Test sent to state laboratory: if negative you will not 
hear from anyone.  If positive, you will be contacted to have 
your baby re-tested at physician

Nursing Management: Early Newborn Period: Discharge Preparation
 Preparing for discharge
 Wrap-unwrap
 Bathing:
 Sponge bath until cord falls off
 Careful with tub bath:  monitor temperature-no running water
 Back to Sleep
 Car seat Safety-car seat check at any fire department
 Skin care- no perfumes, mild soap 
 Infant follow-up: Immunizations- Hep B may be given in hospital
 Education- What to expect-
 Newborn sleep/wake patterns
 When to call the doctor
 High pitched crying that doesn’t stop
 Fever
 Decreased urinary output ( 6- 8 wet diapers after 1st week of life)
 Cultural considerations
 Safe to go outside?
 Siblings? 
 Avoid anyone with illness
 Maternal rest and family bonding: Can’t spoil a baby.  If infant cries you should comfort

Newborn Feeding and Elimination
 Newborn feeding-breast on demand, no time limits
Bottle feeding 15ml per feeding for first day of life
 Increase slowly – 2 oz at 1 week of li
 Newborn elimination
 Voiding: 6 to 8 wet diapers a day at age 1 week.
 Infant Stool-what goes in comes out

Diaper Care
 Change frequently-disposable diapers may not seem wet
 Parent education-stool & urine frequency
 Prevention of diaper rash-change when wet, A&D barrier
 Gentle soap-don’t over bathe
 Fragrance/additive free laundry detergent
